CVE-2026-59766.title: Gitea CVE-2026-20800 sibling endpoints not covered: revoked user still reads private repo objects via `/api/v1/user/starred` and private issue titles via `/api/v1/user/times`
CVE-2026-59766.description:
## Summary
CVE-2026-20800 fixed private-info leakage to revoked users only for the notification endpoint. Two
sibling endpoints that return data keyed on the caller's own relationship still do not re-check repo
access at output time:
- `GET /api/v1/user/starred` — `getStarredRepos()` computes a per-repo permission but still lists every
  starred repo (no filtering), so the full repo object (`full_name`, `private`, `clone_url`, `ssh_url`)
  of a now-inaccessible private repo is returned.
- `GET /api/v1/user/times` — `ListMyTrackedTimes()` queries by `UserID` only and `LoadAttributes` brings
  in the issue (`title`, `state`), leaking private issue titles after revocation.

## Steps to reproduce
Using the provided reproduction materials, as a revoked user:
1. Control: `GET /api/v1/repos/admin/starred-test` → **404**.
2. `GET /api/v1/user/starred` → leaks `admin/starred-test`, `private:true`, `clone_url`.
3. `GET /api/v1/user/times` → leaks `issue.title = "SECRET: …"`, `state`.

(Runtime-confirmed on `gitea/gitea:1.25.4`. Oracle = planted sentinel title; no real secret exfiltrated.)

## Impact
A former collaborator can enumerate private repos they starred and read private issue titles they logged
time on, indefinitely after access revocation. Metadata only (no repo content / comment bodies). Low.

## Suggested remediation
1. `getStarredRepos`: drop (or minimally redact) repos where `permission.HasAnyUnitAccessOrPublicAccess()`
   is false for the caller.
2. `ListMyTrackedTimes`: filter tracked-time entries by current repo access.
3. Optionally clear a user's stars / time entries for a private repo on revocation.

## Credit
Reported as part of an incomplete-patch measurement study (responsible disclosure).

CVE-2026-60008.title: Jupyter notebook renderer emits attacker-controlled CSS classes into unsanitized, unsandboxed output
CVE-2026-60008.description: `modules/markup/jupyter/jupyter.go` sets `SanitizerDisabled: true` but leaves `DisplayInIframe` and `ContentSandbox` at their zero values. It is the only renderer in the tree that turns the sanitizer off while still rendering into the main document. Within that unsanitized output it interpolates `notebook.metadata.language_info.name` — a value read directly from the file — into a literal `class` attribute without routing it through `RenderInternal.FormatWithSafeAttrs`. HTML-escaping prevents closing the attribute, but whitespace is untouched, so the notebook can choose its own list of CSS classes on a page where nothing filters them. Combined with Fomantic's `.ui.dimmer` and Gitea's `!important` Tailwind layer, a repository file can replace the entire viewport of a repository page and intercept clicks on it. Script execution was not reached. The reason to fix this is not the overlay: it is that the class attribute is the one place on this path where a security control was skipped, and there is no sanitizer, no iframe sandbox and no CSP behind it. ## Why this is a boundary failure rather than a cosmetic bug Gitea has a deliberate mechanism to stop rendered content from choosing CSS classes. `RenderInternal.ProtectSafeAttrs` rewrites `class='X'` into `data-attr-class='<per-render-nonce>:X'`; the sanitizer allows `data-attr-class`; and `finalProcessor.Close` converts it back only when the nonce matches. Content cannot forge the nonce, so only the renderer's own trusted code can emit a class. `orgmode.go` uses this correctly: ```go _ = ctx.RenderInternal.FormatWithSafeAttrs(sb, `<pre><code class='chroma language-%s'>`, ...) ``` The intent is also written down inside the affected file itself, in the `text/html` MIME handler: ```go // To future developers: don't allow custom CSS classes or attributes, // because '.link-action' or 'data-fetch-xxx' can send POST requests and lead to XSS. ``` That rule is enforced for MIME output and missed for the language field. ## Details **1. The sanitizer is disabled and the output is not confined.** ```go func (renderer) GetExternalRendererOptions() markup.ExternalRendererOptions { return markup.ExternalRendererOptions{ SanitizerDisabled: true, } } ``` `DisplayInIframe` and `ContentSandbox` are left unset. In `modules/markup/render.go` that removes `SanitizeReader` from the pipeline, and the bytes land inside `<div class='file-view markup jupyter-render'>` on the ordinary repository page. By contrast the `openapi-swagger`, `viewer-3d` and `asciicast` renderers also disable the sanitizer, but set `DisplayInIframe: true` and `ContentSandbox: setting.MarkupRenderDefaultSandbox`, so their output is confined to an iframe with no `allow-same-origin`. **2. Untrusted input reaches a literal `class` attribute.** The `language` value comes from `notebook.metadata.language_info.name`, falling back to `metadata.kernelspec.language`, and is interpolated into a `class='chroma language-…'` attribute. `htmlutil.WriteFormat` applies `template.HTMLEscapeString`, which handles `< > & ' '` and leaves whitespace alone. No input yields a raw `'`, so no new attribute can be created — but spaces pass through, which is enough to append arbitrary additional CSS classes. **3. `/render/` serves the same content with no CSP.** The `/render/` route adds a `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox …` header only when the renderer sets `ContentSandbox`, a field the Jupyter renderer never sets. The result is a top-level, same-origin, navigable `text/html` document built from repository content, with the sanitizer off and no restrictions, reachable anonymously on public repositories. Repository authorization on the route itself is sound (private repositories return 404 to unauthorized users). **4. The notebook selects which frontend renderer processes it.** Because the class is built as `language-%s` from the file, a notebook can declare `'language_info': {'name': 'mermaid'}` (or `math`) and hand its cell source to mermaid.js / KaTeX. Those frontend paths assign markup via `innerHTML` in the parent document before moving it into a non-sandboxed iframe. Today mermaid's `securityLevel: 'strict'` and KaTeX's `trust: false` hold, so script execution was not achieved — but this is the same unsanitized, no-CSP surface, reached from a file type where nothing signals that a diagram will be drawn. ## Impact Anyone with write access to a repository can make its pages display arbitrary full-screen content on the Gitea origin, with the real hostname and certificate, and make the underlying page unusable. Pushed to a shared repository, it affects every colleague who opens that repository, with no link sent and no unusual action taken — making fake session-expiry notices, credential-rotation instructions or outage banners credible because the instance itself serves them. Two bounds are worth stating explicitly: - **It does not cross a permission boundary.** The attacker needs write access to the repository holding the notebook; read-only access is not enough. Existing repository permissions are respected. - **The overlay is text.** The cell body passes through chroma, so there is no input, button or link. A credential prompt must end in 'go to this other host', which the victim types by hand. ## Remediation Upgrade to a fixed release. Until then, avoid rendering or serving untrusted `.ipynb` files (for example by disabling the Jupyter renderer on instances that accept notebooks from untrusted contributors). ## Reporter Toprak Yagcioglu. Found and reproduced against a local throwaway `gitea/gitea:1.27.1` container; nothing was tested against any third-party or production instance. Happy to supply a reproduction and to verify a candidate patch.

CVE-2026-60010.title: Repo-side team-link endpoint still bypasses RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess
CVE-2026-60010.description: ### Summary `PUT /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/teams/{team}` allows a non-owner repository admin to attach organization teams to a repository even when the organization has disabled that behaviour with `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess=false`. An earlier advisory fixed the corresponding team-side endpoint; the repository-side endpoint retained the weaker check. ### Details The repository-side handler's exception relies on a repository permission check (`IsOwner()`), which for an organization repository is satisfied by a user promoted to owner-level access through an attached admin team. The fixed team-side endpoint instead checks actual organization ownership when `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess` is disabled. The matching web collaboration-settings handler had the same weak check. ### Impact A user with delegated admin rights on one organization repository can grant other organization teams read or write access to that repository without approval from an actual organization owner, exposing private source and history and, for a write-capable team, granting push access. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39046, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-60018.title: Authenticated DoS in OneDev migration via unbounded version response body
CVE-2026-60018.description: ### Summary The OneDev migration downloader reads the entire `/~api/version/server` response body into memory before validating the version string, and the migration HTTP client has no timeout. A malicious OneDev-compatible server can return a very large or never-ending response. ### Details Reachable from the web, API and background-task migration paths. Reachable by any authenticated user who can start a repository migration. ### Impact Authenticated availability. An attacker who can start migrations against a server they control can force Gitea to read arbitrarily large response bodies, hold migration requests and workers open until timeout or cancellation, retain that data in memory, and exhaust the migration worker pool. On constrained deployments this creates memory pressure and a possible out-of-memory condition. ### Affected versions Gitea `>= 1.16.0, <= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39024, #39033). ### Workarounds Restrict repository-migration permission to trusted users. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-63792.title: Fork pull requests can read reusable workflow files from another private repository (missed sibling of GHSA-fj8v-hjwv-qm88)
CVE-2026-63792.description: ### Summary `CanReadWorkflowCrossRepo` decides whether an Actions run may read a reusable workflow file referenced from another repository. Its 'collaborative owner' branch grants cross-repository read through the collaborative-owner trust relationship without checking whether the run is a fork pull request. An earlier advisory fixed the same class of flaw in a sibling function but did not touch this one. ### Details A fork pull request opened against private repository A (no write access to A required) can read reusable workflow file contents of a different private repository B, at any git ref, provided A is private, B's Actions configuration lists A's owner as a collaborative owner (a normal use of the reusable-workflow sharing feature), and the fork pull request run is approved and runs. The workflow file path is confined to the configured workflow directories, but the git ref is caller-controlled. ### Impact Read-only disclosure of private reusable workflow file contents. No write access or code execution is granted by this issue. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66849.title: Package registry: restricted users can read packages of limited-visibility users (authorization bypass)
CVE-2026-66849.description: ### Summary The package-registry access check grants read access to a package owned by a Limited-visibility user to any non-ghost logged-in user, without excluding restricted accounts. A restricted account can therefore enumerate and download the entire package registry (for example Docker, npm, PyPI) of any Limited-visibility user. ### Details The user-owner branch of `determineAccessMode` omits the restricted-user check that the organization-owner branch and the repository permission model apply. ### Impact Authorization boundary / confidentiality. A restricted account can read package content of Limited-visibility users that it should not be able to see. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39043, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-70357.title: Gitea validates a repository migration hostname against its netwo ...
CVE-2026-70357.description: Gitea validates a repository migration hostname against its network allow and block lists before invoking Git, but the Git subprocess independently resolves the hostname when connecting. An attacker who can start a migration and control the destination's DNS can change the address between validation and connection to reach a blocked internal address. The affected path is the Git clone operation; validation in the migration HTTP client's dialer does not protect the independently connecting Git subprocess.

CVE-2026-70402.title: Permissive Git hook directory and script modes may allow local code execution as the Gitea service account
CVE-2026-70402.description: ### Summary Gitea creates server-side Git hook directories and scripts with mode `0777`, relying on the process umask to reduce it. Under a permissive umask (for example `0000` or `0002`) the resulting files or directories are group- or world-writable. On a deployment where another local principal can reach the repository storage, that principal can modify an existing hook or add an executable file to a writable hook directory; a later Git operation then runs it as the Gitea service account. ### Details The hook-creation function is reached through ordinary operations (creating or forking a repository, completing a migration, converting a mirror, synchronizing hooks, creating a wiki). A standard systemd deployment with umask `0022` produces mode `0755` and is not directly affected. This does not by itself grant root unless Gitea runs as root. ### Impact Local code execution as the Gitea service account on affected deployments, with the consequences that account allows (modifying repositories, reading accessible files, persistence through hooks). ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39008, #39016). ### Workarounds Run Gitea with a restrictive umask (`0022` or tighter) and ensure repository storage is not writable by untrusted local users. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-70406.title: Public-only tokens can read private head repositories via compare and pull request creation (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-58443)
CVE-2026-70406.description: ### Summary The fix for CVE-2026-58443 added a 'token can access repository' check to `UpdatePullRequest` only. The shared helper `parseCompareInfo`, used by the compare-diff endpoint and by pull request creation, lacked the same check. A `public-only, read:repository` token can read commit history and diff content of a private head repository by routing the request through a public base repository. ### Details The route-level public-only middleware validates only the base repository named in the route. The head repository resolved inside `parseCompareInfo` is checked for user permission but not against the token's scope. Two entry points reach it: 1. `GET /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/compare/{basehead}` with `head` given as `owner/repo:branch`. The head repository does not need to be a fork of the base. 2. `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls` with the same `head` syntax. Gitea then pushes the private head branch to `refs/pull/{index}/head` of the public base repository, where the public diff and patch endpoints serve it. The related disclosure of private head repository metadata and commit SHA through `ToAPIPullRequest` in the pull request read endpoints is handled separately in https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39167. ### Impact Confidentiality bypass of the `public-only` token boundary. A leaked public-only token can read private repository commits and diffs it was explicitly restricted from. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 by https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39006 and https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39013. ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-71184.title: Gitea Actions: fork pull request approval bypass via `pull_request_review_comment` (missing `WithPullRequest`)
CVE-2026-71184.description: ### Summary Gitea requires maintainer approval before running fork pull request workflows when the author lacks Actions write on the base repository. That gate is skipped for the `pull_request_review_comment` event (the same code path also covers review approved/rejected), because the review notifier does not attach the pull request to the notification. With no pull request attached the run is not recognized as a fork pull request and approval is not required, while the workflow definition is still loaded from the fork head and run on the base repository's runners. ### Details The sibling review-request notifier does attach the pull request; the review notifier does not. Present since the fork pull request approval gate was introduced in Gitea 1.20.0. An actor needs to be able to fork the repository, open a fork pull request, and submit a review with a line comment; they do not need Actions write on the base repository or a runner on the fork. ### Impact Unapproved execution of attacker-controlled workflow code on the base repository's runners. On a privileged or host runner this is code execution as the runner user, with possible access to secrets depending on event rules; on a sandboxed runner it is unauthorized CI/compute use. ### Affected versions Gitea `>= 1.20.0, <= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds Instances that do not run fork pull request workflows on self-hosted runners are not exposed to the code-execution impact. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-71301.title: Wiki-only members can read private pull request titles through markup preview
CVE-2026-71301.description: ### Summary In a private repository, a member with only Wiki access can use `POST /{owner}/{repo}/markup` to resolve a same-repository pull request reference and receive the pull request title and state icon, despite having no Issues or Pull Requests access. ### Details The markup route accepts any one of Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Releases or Wiki access. The renderer's unit check for referenced issues and pull requests is applied only in the cross-repository branch, so a same-repository reference reaches title and icon rendering without a unit check. No bodies, comments or attachments are returned. ### Impact Confidentiality. A Wiki-only member can read pull request titles and displayed state from a private repository. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39045, #39054). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73278.title: Gitea's OAuth2 and OpenID Connect sign-in paths do not require a  ...
CVE-2026-73278.description: Gitea's OAuth2 and OpenID Connect sign-in paths do not require a WebAuthn challenge when WebAuthn is the account's only configured second factor. A party able to authenticate through the affected external identity flow can obtain a full session without the passkey verification enforced during password login. One affected path can also persist an external identity link, extending the compromise beyond the initial session; accounts with TOTP configured are outside the reported WebAuthn-only scenario.

CVE-2026-73504.title: Unauthenticated artifact-to-repository oracle in raw Actions downloads
CVE-2026-73504.description: ### Summary The raw Actions artifact download endpoint looks up the artifact row before validating the signed URL. Without authentication, an invalid signature produces one response when the supplied global artifact ID belongs to the named repository (and is upload-confirmed or expired) and a different response when it does not. Because artifact IDs are global auto-incrementing integers, this lets an unauthenticated caller test whether a guessed artifact ID belongs to an already-named private repository. ### Details The signature check still protects artifact bytes; only the ordering of the row lookup and the signature check creates the distinguishable responses. The endpoint does not reveal whether the repository exists, since inaccessible and nonexistent repositories return the same status. ### Impact Unauthenticated confirmation of the association between an artifact ID and a known private repository. Artifact contents are not exposed. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39049, #39053). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73535.title: 2FA bypass and persistent account takeover via OpenID identity linking
CVE-2026-73535.description: The `POST /user/openid/connect` handler did not enforce second-factor authentication. An attacker who knew a victim's password could obtain a full authenticated session by submitting that password through the OpenID connect flow instead of the normal login form, bypassing TOTP and WebAuthn checks entirely. The same request could attach an attacker-controlled OpenID identifier to the victim's account before sign-in completed. Because the OpenID sign-in path also lacked a second-factor check, the attacker could subsequently authenticate using that identifier alone — without the victim's password or second factor. Changing the victim's password did not remove the linked identifier. OpenID sign-in is enabled by default on instances set up through the installer. ## Affected Versions Confirmed on **1.27.1**. All versions that expose the OpenID connect endpoint and support TOTP or WebAuthn second factors should be assumed affected until verified otherwise. ## Impact **Who was affected:** Users on instances with OpenID sign-in enabled who had enrolled TOTP or WebAuthn as a second factor. **What broke:** Second-factor enrollment is intended to make a leaked password survivable. The OpenID connect path removed that protection for enrolled users. Password-based login continued to enforce the second-factor challenge as expected. **Persistent access:** The connect handler wrote the attacker's OpenID identifier to the victim's account before granting the session. Subsequent OpenID sign-ins using that identifier required neither the victim's password nor a second factor. Password rotation did not revoke this access; the linked identifier had to be removed manually from account settings. **`TWO_FACTOR_AUTH = enforced` did not mitigate this.** The enforced setting relied on a session flag set at sign-in time. Because enrolled users were flagged as having completed second-factor setup, hijacked sessions passed the enforced check rather than being challenged again. | Attack vector | Prerequisites | Consequence | |---------------|---------------|-------------| | OpenID connect with password | Victim's password; OpenID sign-in enabled | Full session without second-factor challenge | | OpenID sign-in via linked identifier | Prior successful connect attack | Full session without password or second factor; survives password change | On a compromised Gitea account, an attacker gained access to repositories, CI secrets, Actions configuration, and push permissions for everything the user could write to. Administrator accounts exposed the entire instance. ## Root Cause `ConnectOpenIDPost` (`routers/web/auth/openid.go`) authenticated the user with `auth.UserSignIn`, discarded the returned authentication source (which carries the second-factor policy), linked a new OpenID identifier to the account, and called `handleSignIn` — none of which consulted TOTP or WebAuthn enrollment. The password login handler (`SignInPost` in `routers/web/auth/auth.go`) checked `TwoFactorShouldSkip()`, TOTP enrollment, and WebAuthn registration before granting a session. Those checks were absent from the OpenID connect flow. OpenID 2.0 identities are stored in the `user_openid` table rather than as a configurable authentication source, so there was no per-source setting that could explain the missing enforcement.

CVE-2026-78231.title: Unauthenticated Blind SSRF via OpenID Sign-In Verification
CVE-2026-78231.description: ### Summary When OpenID sign-in is enabled, Gitea accepts an unauthenticated GET request to `/user/login/openid` and passes attacker-controlled OpenID assertion parameters into the OpenID 2.0 verification flow. During verification, the upstream `github.com/yohcop/openid-go` library sends a server-side `POST` request to the attacker-controlled `openid.op_endpoint` URL using `http.DefaultClient`. This gives an unauthenticated remote attacker a blind SSRF primitive from the Gitea server. The attacker controls the destination URL and the form-encoded POST body. In deployments where the Gitea server can reach loopback, private-network, link-local, or otherwise internal HTTP services, this can be used to interact with services that are not directly reachable by the attacker. ### Details The vulnerable route is the OpenID sign-in endpoint: ```go m.Combo('/login/openid'). Get(auth.SignInOpenID). Post(web.Bind(forms.SignInOpenIDForm{}), auth.SignInOpenIDPost) ``` The route is gated by `openIDSignInEnabled`, but it does not require an authenticated user. When `[openid] ENABLE_OPENID_SIGNIN = true`, an anonymous client can reach the GET handler. ### Impact An attacker can cause the Gitea server to send an outbound HTTP POST request to an attacker-controlled URL by sending one unauthenticated GET request to `/user/login/openid`, provided OpenID sign-in is enabled. The attacker controls the target URL through `openid.op_endpoint` and controls much of the form-encoded body through the supplied OpenID query parameters. The impact depends on the deployment environment and network reachability. In common self-hosted deployments, Gitea may be able to reach services that are not exposed to the internet, including loopback services, internal admin panels, CI/CD endpoints, internal webhooks, private-network APIs, or link-local metadata endpoints. Because the response is not returned to the attacker, the primitive is blind, but it can still trigger state-changing actions on internal services that accept POST requests, and it can be used as an internal network interaction primitive. This also creates an availability risk if outbound requests can be made to slow or non-responsive targets, because the OpenID path uses the default HTTP client behavior without an apparent request timeout in this path. I would honestly argue that a higher environmental score may be appropriate where the Gitea server can reach sensitive unauthenticated internal services that accept form-encoded POST requests.

CVE-2026-78433.title: Attachments created before the January 2026 cutoff skip the cross repository check entirely, and permission is then evaluated against the repository named in the URL rather than the repository owning the attachment, so a private repository's attachment is served through any public repository's path
CVE-2026-78433.description: ### Summary The web attachment handler contains a guard that rejects a request for an attachment made through a repository other than the one that owns it. That guard is applied only to attachments created after 16 January 2026; older attachments skip it even when their owning-repository id is correctly populated. When the guard is skipped, the handler evaluates permission against the repository named in the request URL instead of the repository that owns the attachment. An attachment belonging to a private repository can therefore be retrieved by requesting it through any public repository's attachment path. The route allows anonymous access, so no authentication is required. ### Details In `routers/web/repo/attachment.go` the cross-repository check is gated only on the attachment's creation timestamp, unlike its two sibling call sites which also require the owning-repository id to be unset. A migration backfills that id on upgrade, so the timestamp-only exemption protects no legitimate rows and instead allows permission to be checked against the wrong repository. Downstream draft-release and token-scope checks inherit the same wrong subject. Attachment UUIDs are random and not enumerable, so exploitation requires knowledge of a specific attachment UUID (for example from a removed collaborator, a public-to-private conversion, notification mail, webhook payloads, or proxy/CDN logs). ### Impact Disclosure of private-repository attachment contents — issue and pull request attachments and release assets — to an unauthenticated caller who knows the attachment UUID. Incorrect authorization / cross-repository access control bypass. Affects any instance that held attachments created before 16 January 2026. ### Affected versions Gitea `>= 1.26.0, <= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39048, #39077). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

GHSA-m984-2424-x6vw.title: Generic attachment downloads bypass draft-release visibility checks
GHSA-m984-2424-x6vw.description: ### Summary In Gitea 1.26.1, anonymous users can download draft release assets through `/attachments/{uuid}` even when the draft release itself is hidden. The generic attachment route does not re-apply the draft-release visibility check before serving the file. ### Details The verified report ties this to `routers/web/repo/attachment.go:141-173`, which serves linked attachments without reloading the parent release or enforcing the draft flag again. `routers/api/v1/repo/release_attachment.go:23-40,134-150` shows the normal release path does enforce `canAccessReleaseDraft(ctx)`, while `services/repository/repository.go:199-204` collapses release attachments down to `unit.TypeReleases` and loses the `IsDraft` context. `routers/web/web.go:872,1471` routes UUID-based attachment downloads to the generic handler. In the verified test, anonymous access to the draft release API returned `404`, but anonymous access to `/attachments/{uuid}` returned `200` and served the draft asset content. ### PoC 1. Start an isolated Gitea 1.26.1 instance and set `BASE=http://127.0.0.1:3000`. Create a test user `owner`. 2. As `owner`, create a public initialized repository: `curl -u owner:ownerpass123 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{'name':'draft-asset-demo','private':false,'auto_init':true}' '$BASE/api/v1/user/repos'` 3. As `owner`, create a draft release and copy the returned numeric release ID: `curl -u owner:ownerpass123 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{'tag_name':'draft-1','name':'draft-1','draft':true}' '$BASE/api/v1/repos/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases'` 4. Create a harmless asset with recognizable content: `printf 'draft-only-binary' > /tmp/draft-asset.txt` 5. Upload it to the draft release and copy the returned `uuid` or `browser_download_url`: `curl -u owner:ownerpass123 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' --data-binary @/tmp/draft-asset.txt '$BASE/api/v1/repos/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases/$RELEASE_ID/assets?name=draft-asset.txt'` 6. As an anonymous user with no cookies, verify the draft release itself is hidden: `curl -i '$BASE/api/v1/repos/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases/$RELEASE_ID'` 7. Confirm this returns `404`. 8. As the same anonymous user, request the generic attachment route: `curl -i '$BASE/attachments/$UUID'` 9. Observe `200 OK` and the file body `draft-only-binary`. 10. Optionally compare with the normal release download route `/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases/download/draft-1/draft-asset.txt`, which should remain hidden while `/attachments/$UUID` succeeds. ### Impact This leaks unpublished release assets. Anyone who learns the attachment UUID can retrieve draft binaries or other release files before the maintainer chooses to publish them.

CVE-2026-59766.title: Gitea CVE-2026-20800 sibling endpoints not covered: revoked user still reads private repo objects via `/api/v1/user/starred` and private issue titles via `/api/v1/user/times`
CVE-2026-59766.description:
## Summary
CVE-2026-20800 fixed private-info leakage to revoked users only for the notification endpoint. Two
sibling endpoints that return data keyed on the caller's own relationship still do not re-check repo
access at output time:
- `GET /api/v1/user/starred` — `getStarredRepos()` computes a per-repo permission but still lists every
  starred repo (no filtering), so the full repo object (`full_name`, `private`, `clone_url`, `ssh_url`)
  of a now-inaccessible private repo is returned.
- `GET /api/v1/user/times` — `ListMyTrackedTimes()` queries by `UserID` only and `LoadAttributes` brings
  in the issue (`title`, `state`), leaking private issue titles after revocation.

## Steps to reproduce
Using the provided reproduction materials, as a revoked user:
1. Control: `GET /api/v1/repos/admin/starred-test` → **404**.
2. `GET /api/v1/user/starred` → leaks `admin/starred-test`, `private:true`, `clone_url`.
3. `GET /api/v1/user/times` → leaks `issue.title = "SECRET: …"`, `state`.

(Runtime-confirmed on `gitea/gitea:1.25.4`. Oracle = planted sentinel title; no real secret exfiltrated.)

## Impact
A former collaborator can enumerate private repos they starred and read private issue titles they logged
time on, indefinitely after access revocation. Metadata only (no repo content / comment bodies). Low.

## Suggested remediation
1. `getStarredRepos`: drop (or minimally redact) repos where `permission.HasAnyUnitAccessOrPublicAccess()`
   is false for the caller.
2. `ListMyTrackedTimes`: filter tracked-time entries by current repo access.
3. Optionally clear a user's stars / time entries for a private repo on revocation.

## Credit
Reported as part of an incomplete-patch measurement study (responsible disclosure).

CVE-2026-60008.title: Jupyter notebook renderer emits attacker-controlled CSS classes into unsanitized, unsandboxed output
CVE-2026-60008.description: `modules/markup/jupyter/jupyter.go` sets `SanitizerDisabled: true` but leaves `DisplayInIframe` and `ContentSandbox` at their zero values. It is the only renderer in the tree that turns the sanitizer off while still rendering into the main document. Within that unsanitized output it interpolates `notebook.metadata.language_info.name` — a value read directly from the file — into a literal `class` attribute without routing it through `RenderInternal.FormatWithSafeAttrs`. HTML-escaping prevents closing the attribute, but whitespace is untouched, so the notebook can choose its own list of CSS classes on a page where nothing filters them. Combined with Fomantic's `.ui.dimmer` and Gitea's `!important` Tailwind layer, a repository file can replace the entire viewport of a repository page and intercept clicks on it. Script execution was not reached. The reason to fix this is not the overlay: it is that the class attribute is the one place on this path where a security control was skipped, and there is no sanitizer, no iframe sandbox and no CSP behind it. ## Why this is a boundary failure rather than a cosmetic bug Gitea has a deliberate mechanism to stop rendered content from choosing CSS classes. `RenderInternal.ProtectSafeAttrs` rewrites `class='X'` into `data-attr-class='<per-render-nonce>:X'`; the sanitizer allows `data-attr-class`; and `finalProcessor.Close` converts it back only when the nonce matches. Content cannot forge the nonce, so only the renderer's own trusted code can emit a class. `orgmode.go` uses this correctly: ```go _ = ctx.RenderInternal.FormatWithSafeAttrs(sb, `<pre><code class='chroma language-%s'>`, ...) ``` The intent is also written down inside the affected file itself, in the `text/html` MIME handler: ```go // To future developers: don't allow custom CSS classes or attributes, // because '.link-action' or 'data-fetch-xxx' can send POST requests and lead to XSS. ``` That rule is enforced for MIME output and missed for the language field. ## Details **1. The sanitizer is disabled and the output is not confined.** ```go func (renderer) GetExternalRendererOptions() markup.ExternalRendererOptions { return markup.ExternalRendererOptions{ SanitizerDisabled: true, } } ``` `DisplayInIframe` and `ContentSandbox` are left unset. In `modules/markup/render.go` that removes `SanitizeReader` from the pipeline, and the bytes land inside `<div class='file-view markup jupyter-render'>` on the ordinary repository page. By contrast the `openapi-swagger`, `viewer-3d` and `asciicast` renderers also disable the sanitizer, but set `DisplayInIframe: true` and `ContentSandbox: setting.MarkupRenderDefaultSandbox`, so their output is confined to an iframe with no `allow-same-origin`. **2. Untrusted input reaches a literal `class` attribute.** The `language` value comes from `notebook.metadata.language_info.name`, falling back to `metadata.kernelspec.language`, and is interpolated into a `class='chroma language-…'` attribute. `htmlutil.WriteFormat` applies `template.HTMLEscapeString`, which handles `< > & ' '` and leaves whitespace alone. No input yields a raw `'`, so no new attribute can be created — but spaces pass through, which is enough to append arbitrary additional CSS classes. **3. `/render/` serves the same content with no CSP.** The `/render/` route adds a `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox …` header only when the renderer sets `ContentSandbox`, a field the Jupyter renderer never sets. The result is a top-level, same-origin, navigable `text/html` document built from repository content, with the sanitizer off and no restrictions, reachable anonymously on public repositories. Repository authorization on the route itself is sound (private repositories return 404 to unauthorized users). **4. The notebook selects which frontend renderer processes it.** Because the class is built as `language-%s` from the file, a notebook can declare `'language_info': {'name': 'mermaid'}` (or `math`) and hand its cell source to mermaid.js / KaTeX. Those frontend paths assign markup via `innerHTML` in the parent document before moving it into a non-sandboxed iframe. Today mermaid's `securityLevel: 'strict'` and KaTeX's `trust: false` hold, so script execution was not achieved — but this is the same unsanitized, no-CSP surface, reached from a file type where nothing signals that a diagram will be drawn. ## Impact Anyone with write access to a repository can make its pages display arbitrary full-screen content on the Gitea origin, with the real hostname and certificate, and make the underlying page unusable. Pushed to a shared repository, it affects every colleague who opens that repository, with no link sent and no unusual action taken — making fake session-expiry notices, credential-rotation instructions or outage banners credible because the instance itself serves them. Two bounds are worth stating explicitly: - **It does not cross a permission boundary.** The attacker needs write access to the repository holding the notebook; read-only access is not enough. Existing repository permissions are respected. - **The overlay is text.** The cell body passes through chroma, so there is no input, button or link. A credential prompt must end in 'go to this other host', which the victim types by hand. ## Remediation Upgrade to a fixed release. Until then, avoid rendering or serving untrusted `.ipynb` files (for example by disabling the Jupyter renderer on instances that accept notebooks from untrusted contributors). ## Reporter Toprak Yagcioglu. Found and reproduced against a local throwaway `gitea/gitea:1.27.1` container; nothing was tested against any third-party or production instance. Happy to supply a reproduction and to verify a candidate patch.

CVE-2026-60010.title: Repo-side team-link endpoint still bypasses RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess
CVE-2026-60010.description: ### Summary `PUT /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/teams/{team}` allows a non-owner repository admin to attach organization teams to a repository even when the organization has disabled that behaviour with `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess=false`. An earlier advisory fixed the corresponding team-side endpoint; the repository-side endpoint retained the weaker check. ### Details The repository-side handler's exception relies on a repository permission check (`IsOwner()`), which for an organization repository is satisfied by a user promoted to owner-level access through an attached admin team. The fixed team-side endpoint instead checks actual organization ownership when `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess` is disabled. The matching web collaboration-settings handler had the same weak check. ### Impact A user with delegated admin rights on one organization repository can grant other organization teams read or write access to that repository without approval from an actual organization owner, exposing private source and history and, for a write-capable team, granting push access. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39046, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-60018.title: Authenticated DoS in OneDev migration via unbounded version response body
CVE-2026-60018.description: ### Summary The OneDev migration downloader reads the entire `/~api/version/server` response body into memory before validating the version string, and the migration HTTP client has no timeout. A malicious OneDev-compatible server can return a very large or never-ending response. ### Details Reachable from the web, API and background-task migration paths. Reachable by any authenticated user who can start a repository migration. ### Impact Authenticated availability. An attacker who can start migrations against a server they control can force Gitea to read arbitrarily large response bodies, hold migration requests and workers open until timeout or cancellation, retain that data in memory, and exhaust the migration worker pool. On constrained deployments this creates memory pressure and a possible out-of-memory condition. ### Affected versions Gitea `>= 1.16.0, <= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39024, #39033). ### Workarounds Restrict repository-migration permission to trusted users. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-63792.title: Fork pull requests can read reusable workflow files from another private repository (missed sibling of GHSA-fj8v-hjwv-qm88)
CVE-2026-63792.description: ### Summary `CanReadWorkflowCrossRepo` decides whether an Actions run may read a reusable workflow file referenced from another repository. Its 'collaborative owner' branch grants cross-repository read through the collaborative-owner trust relationship without checking whether the run is a fork pull request. An earlier advisory fixed the same class of flaw in a sibling function but did not touch this one. ### Details A fork pull request opened against private repository A (no write access to A required) can read reusable workflow file contents of a different private repository B, at any git ref, provided A is private, B's Actions configuration lists A's owner as a collaborative owner (a normal use of the reusable-workflow sharing feature), and the fork pull request run is approved and runs. The workflow file path is confined to the configured workflow directories, but the git ref is caller-controlled. ### Impact Read-only disclosure of private reusable workflow file contents. No write access or code execution is granted by this issue. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66849.title: Package registry: restricted users can read packages of limited-visibility users (authorization bypass)
CVE-2026-66849.description: ### Summary The package-registry access check grants read access to a package owned by a Limited-visibility user to any non-ghost logged-in user, without excluding restricted accounts. A restricted account can therefore enumerate and download the entire package registry (for example Docker, npm, PyPI) of any Limited-visibility user. ### Details The user-owner branch of `determineAccessMode` omits the restricted-user check that the organization-owner branch and the repository permission model apply. ### Impact Authorization boundary / confidentiality. A restricted account can read package content of Limited-visibility users that it should not be able to see. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39043, #39058). ### Workarounds None. CVE-2026-70402.title: Permissive Git hook directory and script modes may allow local code execution as the Gitea service account
CVE-2026-70402.description: ### Summary Gitea creates server-side Git hook directories and scripts with mode `0777`, relying on the process umask to reduce it. Under a permissive umask (for example `0000` or `0002`) the resulting files or directories are group- or world-writable. On a deployment where another local principal can reach the repository storage, that principal can modify an existing hook or add an executable file to a writable hook directory; a later Git operation then runs it as the Gitea service account. ### Details The hook-creation function is reached through ordinary operations (creating or forking a repository, completing a migration, converting a mirror, synchronizing hooks, creating a wiki). A standard systemd deployment with umask `0022` produces mode `0755` and is not directly affected. This does not by itself grant root unless Gitea runs as root. ### Impact Local code execution as the Gitea service account on affected deployments, with the consequences that account allows (modifying repositories, reading accessible files, persistence through hooks). ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39008, #39016). ### Workarounds Run Gitea with a restrictive umask (`0022` or tighter) and ensure repository storage is not writable by untrusted local users. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-70406.title: Public-only tokens can read private head repositories via compare and pull request creation (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-58443)
CVE-2026-70406.description: ### Summary The fix for CVE-2026-58443 added a 'token can access repository' check to `UpdatePullRequest` only. The shared helper `parseCompareInfo`, used by the compare-diff endpoint and by pull request creation, lacked the same check. A `public-only, read:repository` token can read commit history and diff content of a private head repository by routing the request through a public base repository. ### Details The route-level public-only middleware validates only the base repository named in the route. The head repository resolved inside `parseCompareInfo` is checked for user permission but not against the token's scope. Two entry points reach it: 1. `GET /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/compare/{basehead}` with `head` given as `owner/repo:branch`. The head repository does not need to be a fork of the base. 2. `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls` with the same `head` syntax. Gitea then pushes the private head branch to `refs/pull/{index}/head` of the public base repository, where the public diff and patch endpoints serve it. The related disclosure of private head repository metadata and commit SHA through `ToAPIPullRequest` in the pull request read endpoints is handled separately in https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39167. ### Impact Confidentiality bypass of the `public-only` token boundary. A leaked public-only token can read private repository commits and diffs it was explicitly restricted from. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 by https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39006 and https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39013. ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-71184.title: Gitea Actions: fork pull request approval bypass via `pull_request_review_comment` (missing `WithPullRequest`)
CVE-2026-71184.description: ### Summary Gitea requires maintainer approval before running fork pull request workflows when the author lacks Actions write on the base repository. That gate is skipped for the `pull_request_review_comment` event (the same code path also covers review approved/rejected), because the review notifier does not attach the pull request to the notification. With no pull request attached the run is not recognized as a fork pull request and approval is not required, while the workflow definition is still loaded from the fork head and run on the base repository's runners. ### Details The sibling review-request notifier does attach the pull request; the review notifier does not. Present since the fork pull request approval gate was introduced in Gitea 1.20.0. An actor needs to be able to fork the repository, open a fork pull request, and submit a review with a line comment; they do not need Actions write on the base repository or a runner on the fork. ### Impact Unapproved execution of attacker-controlled workflow code on the base repository's runners. On a privileged or host runner this is code execution as the runner user, with possible access to secrets depending on event rules; on a sandboxed runner it is unauthorized CI/compute use. ### Affected versions Gitea `>= 1.20.0, <= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds Instances that do not run fork pull request workflows on self-hosted runners are not exposed to the code-execution impact. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-71301.title: Wiki-only members can read private pull request titles through markup preview
CVE-2026-71301.description: ### Summary In a private repository, a member with only Wiki access can use `POST /{owner}/{repo}/markup` to resolve a same-repository pull request reference and receive the pull request title and state icon, despite having no Issues or Pull Requests access. ### Details The markup route accepts any one of Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Releases or Wiki access. The renderer's unit check for referenced issues and pull requests is applied only in the cross-repository branch, so a same-repository reference reaches title and icon rendering without a unit check. No bodies, comments or attachments are returned. ### Impact Confidentiality. A Wiki-only member can read pull request titles and displayed state from a private repository. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39045, #39054). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73278.title: Gitea's OAuth2 and OpenID Connect sign-in paths do not require a  ...
CVE-2026-73278.description: Gitea's OAuth2 and OpenID Connect sign-in paths do not require a WebAuthn challenge when WebAuthn is the account's only configured second factor. A party able to authenticate through the affected external identity flow can obtain a full session without the passkey verification enforced during password login. One affected path can also persist an external identity link, extending the compromise beyond the initial session; accounts with TOTP configured are outside the reported WebAuthn-only scenario.

CVE-2026-73504.title: Unauthenticated artifact-to-repository oracle in raw Actions downloads
CVE-2026-73504.description: ### Summary The raw Actions artifact download endpoint looks up the artifact row before validating the signed URL. Without authentication, an invalid signature produces one response when the supplied global artifact ID belongs to the named repository (and is upload-confirmed or expired) and a different response when it does not. Because artifact IDs are global auto-incrementing integers, this lets an unauthenticated caller test whether a guessed artifact ID belongs to an already-named private repository. ### Details The signature check still protects artifact bytes; only the ordering of the row lookup and the signature check creates the distinguishable responses. The endpoint does not reveal whether the repository exists, since inaccessible and nonexistent repositories return the same status. ### Impact Unauthenticated confirmation of the association between an artifact ID and a known private repository. Artifact contents are not exposed. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39049, #39053). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73535.title: 2FA bypass and persistent account takeover via OpenID identity linking
CVE-2026-73535.description: The `POST /user/openid/connect` handler did not enforce second-factor authentication. An attacker who knew a victim's password could obtain a full authenticated session by submitting that password through the OpenID connect flow instead of the normal login form, bypassing TOTP and WebAuthn checks entirely. The same request could attach an attacker-controlled OpenID identifier to the victim's account before sign-in completed. Because the OpenID sign-in path also lacked a second-factor check, the attacker could subsequently authenticate using that identifier alone — without the victim's password or second factor. Changing the victim's password did not remove the linked identifier. OpenID sign-in is enabled by default on instances set up through the installer. ## Affected Versions Confirmed on **1.27.1**. All versions that expose the OpenID connect endpoint and support TOTP or WebAuthn second factors should be assumed affected until verified otherwise. ## Impact **Who was affected:** Users on instances with OpenID sign-in enabled who had enrolled TOTP or WebAuthn as a second factor. **What broke:** Second-factor enrollment is intended to make a leaked password survivable. The OpenID connect path removed that protection for enrolled users. Password-based login continued to enforce the second-factor challenge as expected. **Persistent access:** The connect handler wrote the attacker's OpenID identifier to the victim's account before granting the session. Subsequent OpenID sign-ins using that identifier required neither the victim's password nor a second factor. Password rotation did not revoke this access; the linked identifier had to be removed manually from account settings. **`TWO_FACTOR_AUTH = enforced` did not mitigate this.** The enforced setting relied on a session flag set at sign-in time. Because enrolled users were flagged as having completed second-factor setup, hijacked sessions passed the enforced check rather than being challenged again. | Attack vector | Prerequisites | Consequence | |---------------|---------------|-------------| | OpenID connect with password | Victim's password; OpenID sign-in enabled | Full session without second-factor challenge | | OpenID sign-in via linked identifier | Prior successful connect attack | Full session without password or second factor; survives password change | On a compromised Gitea account, an attacker gained access to repositories, CI secrets, Actions configuration, and push permissions for everything the user could write to. Administrator accounts exposed the entire instance. ## Root Cause `ConnectOpenIDPost` (`routers/web/auth/openid.go`) authenticated the user with `auth.UserSignIn`, discarded the returned authentication source (which carries the second-factor policy), linked a new OpenID identifier to the account, and called `handleSignIn` — none of which consulted TOTP or WebAuthn enrollment. The password login handler (`SignInPost` in `routers/web/auth/auth.go`) checked `TwoFactorShouldSkip()`, TOTP enrollment, and WebAuthn registration before granting a session. Those checks were absent from the OpenID connect flow. OpenID 2.0 identities are stored in the `user_openid` table rather than as a configurable authentication source, so there was no per-source setting that could explain the missing enforcement.

CVE-2026-78231.title: Unauthenticated Blind SSRF via OpenID Sign-In Verification
CVE-2026-78231.description: ### Summary When OpenID sign-in is enabled, Gitea accepts an unauthenticated GET request to `/user/login/openid` and passes attacker-controlled OpenID assertion parameters into the OpenID 2.0 verification flow. During verification, the upstream `github.com/yohcop/openid-go` library sends a server-side `POST` request to the attacker-controlled `openid.op_endpoint` URL using `http.DefaultClient`. This gives an unauthenticated remote attacker a blind SSRF primitive from the Gitea server. The attacker controls the destination URL and the form-encoded POST body. In deployments where the Gitea server can reach loopback, private-network, link-local, or otherwise internal HTTP services, this can be used to interact with services that are not directly reachable by the attacker. ### Details The vulnerable route is the OpenID sign-in endpoint: ```go m.Combo('/login/openid'). Get(auth.SignInOpenID). Post(web.Bind(forms.SignInOpenIDForm{}), auth.SignInOpenIDPost) ``` The route is gated by `openIDSignInEnabled`, but it does not require an authenticated user. When `[openid] ENABLE_OPENID_SIGNIN = true`, an anonymous client can reach the GET handler. ### Impact An attacker can cause the Gitea server to send an outbound HTTP POST request to an attacker-controlled URL by sending one unauthenticated GET request to `/user/login/openid`, provided OpenID sign-in is enabled. The attacker controls the target URL through `openid.op_endpoint` and controls much of the form-encoded body through the supplied OpenID query parameters. The impact depends on the deployment environment and network reachability. In common self-hosted deployments, Gitea may be able to reach services that are not exposed to the internet, including loopback services, internal admin panels, CI/CD endpoints, internal webhooks, private-network APIs, or link-local metadata endpoints. Because the response is not returned to the attacker, the primitive is blind, but it can still trigger state-changing actions on internal services that accept POST requests, and it can be used as an internal network interaction primitive. This also creates an availability risk if outbound requests can be made to slow or non-responsive targets, because the OpenID path uses the default HTTP client behavior without an apparent request timeout in this path. I would honestly argue that a higher environmental score may be appropriate where the Gitea server can reach sensitive unauthenticated internal services that accept form-encoded POST requests.

CVE-2026-78433.title: Attachments created before the January 2026 cutoff skip the cross repository check entirely, and permission is then evaluated against the repository named in the URL rather than the repository owning the attachment, so a private repository's attachment is served through any public repository's path
CVE-2026-78433.description: ### Summary The web attachment handler contains a guard that rejects a request for an attachment made through a repository other than the one that owns it. That guard is applied only to attachments created after 16 January 2026; older attachments skip it even when their owning-repository id is correctly populated. When the guard is skipped, the handler evaluates permission against the repository named in the request URL instead of the repository that owns the attachment. An attachment belonging to a private repository can therefore be retrieved by requesting it through any public repository's attachment path. The route allows anonymous access, so no authentication is required. ### Details In `routers/web/repo/attachment.go` the cross-repository check is gated only on the attachment's creation timestamp, unlike its two sibling call sites which also require the owning-repository id to be unset. A migration backfills that id on upgrade, so the timestamp-only exemption protects no legitimate rows and instead allows permission to be checked against the wrong repository. Downstream draft-release and token-scope checks inherit the same wrong subject. Attachment UUIDs are random and not enumerable, so exploitation requires knowledge of a specific attachment UUID (for example from a removed collaborator, a public-to-private conversion, notification mail, webhook payloads, or proxy/CDN logs). ### Impact Disclosure of private-repository attachment contents — issue and pull request attachments and release assets — to an unauthenticated caller who knows the attachment UUID. Incorrect authorization / cross-repository access control bypass. Affects any instance that held attachments created before 16 January 2026. ### Affected versions Gitea `>= 1.26.0, <= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39048, #39077). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-79960.title: When a push was authenticated with a deploy key, Gitea recorded t ...
CVE-2026-79960.description: When a push was authenticated with a deploy key, Gitea recorded the repository owner as the pusher, so permission checks in the push hook pipeline evaluated the owner instead of the deploy key. A holder of a writable deploy key could create protected tags without being on the tag allow list and change repository visibility through push options, for example making a private repository public. Pull requests created through the AGit flow with a deploy key were also attributed to the owner.

CVE-2026-86684.title: The Gitea push mirror API checked whether the repository owner, i ...
CVE-2026-86684.description: The Gitea push mirror API checked whether the repository owner, instead of the requesting user, may use local file system paths. On instances with `[security] IMPORT_LOCAL_PATHS = true`, a repository administrator who is not allowed to import local paths could add a push mirror to a local path on the server when the repository owner has that permission. Gitea then pushed the repository's refs into an existing Git repository at that path with the permissions of the Gitea process.

CVE-2026-89430.title: Gitea validated a push mirror's remote address against the `[migr ...
CVE-2026-89430.description: Gitea validated a push mirror's remote address against the `[migrations]` allow and block lists only when the mirror was created. Each synchronization passed the stored address directly to `git push`, so a name that later resolved to a blocked or internal address was still reached. A user with administrator access to a repository, which includes repositories they create themselves, could aim push mirror synchronization at internal Git services and force-push the repository's contents to them.

CVE-2026-94205.title: Gitea Actions decided whether a fork pull request run needed appr ...
CVE-2026-94205.description: Gitea Actions decided whether a fork pull request run needed approval based on the user who triggered the event rather than the pull request author. For `pull_request` activity triggered by a maintainer during ordinary triage, such as adding a label, the run was created without requiring approval, while the workflow definition was still taken from the fork head. Where Actions is enabled and a matching runner is registered, fork-controlled workflow code could run on the base repository's runners without an explicit approval.

CVE-2026-95106.title: Gitea accepted pushed Git trees containing two entries with the s ...
CVE-2026-95106.description: Gitea accepted pushed Git trees containing two entries with the same name, which Git's own consistency checks reject. Gitea's web views resolved such a path to the first entry, while `git checkout`, Gitea Actions, and release archives use the last. A contributor could open a pull request whose diff and file views show benign content while CI and checkouts at the same commit use different, attacker-controlled content. Incoming objects are now checked for consistency; objects already stored in existing repositories are not rescanned.

CVE-2026-95112.title: When processing issue and comment bodies, Gitea scanned the entir ...
CVE-2026-95112.description: When processing issue and comment bodies, Gitea scanned the entire preceding text for action keywords such as "closes" or "fixes" once per Markdown link, giving processing time quadratic in the input size. An authenticated user able to submit issue or comment content could send a crafted body of about 1 MB that keeps a CPU core busy for several minutes while holding a database transaction open.

CVE-2026-96399.title: A repository's external issue tracker regular expression containi ...
CVE-2026-96399.description: A repository's external issue tracker regular expression containing alternating capture groups could produce invalid slice indexes when Gitea rendered issue references, causing a runtime panic that terminated the Gitea process. A user who can edit a repository's external issue tracker settings could make any later rendering of matching content, such as viewing a README, crash the instance for all users.

CVE-2026-96400.title: With `[migrations] ALLOWED_DOMAINS` set to a matching entry such  ...
CVE-2026-96400.description: With `[migrations] ALLOWED_DOMAINS` set to a matching entry such as `*` or a hostname wildcard, Gitea's migration URL validation could permit reserved and link-local addresses, such as `169.254.169.254`, even when `ALLOW_LOCALNETWORKS = false`. The local-network block list did not cover these ranges, and a hostname matching the allow list was accepted regardless of its resolved address. A user who can start migrations on such an instance could reach these addresses from the Gitea server; the default empty `ALLOWED_DOMAINS` configuration is not affected.

CVE-2026-96404.title: When Gitea's web installer is reachable against a database that a ...
CVE-2026-96404.description: When Gitea's web installer is reachable against a database that already contains users, such as after `INSTALL_LOCK` has been reset to `false`, submitting the install form with an administrator username matching an existing account issued an authenticated session for that account without verifying its password. If the account is an administrator, the session grants full administrative access, including changing the account's password. Databases with a single user also did not require the reinstall confirmation.

CVE-2026-96580.title: Gitea expanded a workflow's static `strategy.matrix` into its ful ...
CVE-2026-96580.description: Gitea expanded a workflow's static `strategy.matrix` into its full Cartesian product without a size limit when creating a run, before the fork pull request approval gate applied. A user who can open a pull request from a fork could submit a small workflow file whose matrix expands to a very large number of jobs, consuming server memory and potentially terminating the Gitea process. No runner is required. Static matrices above 256 combinations are now rejected before expansion.

CVE-2026-96589.title: When a private repository is transferred to a user who lacks acce ...
CVE-2026-96589.description: When a private repository is transferred to a user who lacks access, Gitea grants that recipient temporary read access as a collaborator so they can review the repository. Rejecting or cancelling the transfer did not revoke this collaboration, so the named recipient kept persistent read access to the private repository, including its code, issues, pull requests and wiki, and could clone it. The repository owner was not notified. Transfer-granted access is now removed while collaborations that existed before the transfer are preserved.

CVE-2026-96594.title: The Gitea API endpoint `GET /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/media/{f ...
CVE-2026-96594.description: The Gitea API endpoint `GET /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/media/{filepath}` wrote files of up to 1 KiB that are stored directly in Git, not in LFS, to the response without the content type and disposition headers Gitea uses for user content. An HTML file committed to a repository was therefore rendered by the browser on the Gitea origin. A user who can push to a repository could run JavaScript in the session of a victim who opens the media URL and act with the victim's permissions.

CVE-2026-97208.title: The Gitea API endpoint for creating push mirrors (`POST /api/v1/r ...
CVE-2026-97208.description: The Gitea API endpoint for creating push mirrors (`POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/push_mirrors`) checked only whether mirroring was enabled and not the `[mirror] DISABLE_NEW_PUSH` setting that the web interface enforces. A repository administrator could therefore create new push mirrors on instances where the site administrator had disabled them. A push mirror pushes all refs of the repository to a remote chosen by the caller, on each commit or on a schedule.

CVE-2026-97626.title: Requesting a user or organization profile page (`GET /{username}` ...
CVE-2026-97626.description: Requesting a user or organization profile page (`GET /{username}`) with an `Accept: application/rss+xml` or `Accept: application/atom+xml` header returned the owner's activity feed without the visibility check that the profile page and the `.rss` and `.atom` routes apply. Anonymous users, restricted users and non-members could confirm the existence of limited or private users and private organizations and read their profile details and public activity, also when `[other] ENABLE_FEED` was disabled. Activity in private repositories was not included.

GHSA-m984-2424-x6vw.title: Generic attachment downloads bypass draft-release visibility checks
GHSA-m984-2424-x6vw.description: ### Summary In Gitea 1.26.1, anonymous users can download draft release assets through `/attachments/{uuid}` even when the draft release itself is hidden. The generic attachment route does not re-apply the draft-release visibility check before serving the file. ### Details The verified report ties this to `routers/web/repo/attachment.go:141-173`, which serves linked attachments without reloading the parent release or enforcing the draft flag again. `routers/api/v1/repo/release_attachment.go:23-40,134-150` shows the normal release path does enforce `canAccessReleaseDraft(ctx)`, while `services/repository/repository.go:199-204` collapses release attachments down to `unit.TypeReleases` and loses the `IsDraft` context. `routers/web/web.go:872,1471` routes UUID-based attachment downloads to the generic handler. In the verified test, anonymous access to the draft release API returned `404`, but anonymous access to `/attachments/{uuid}` returned `200` and served the draft asset content. ### PoC 1. Start an isolated Gitea 1.26.1 instance and set `BASE=http://127.0.0.1:3000`. Create a test user `owner`. 2. As `owner`, create a public initialized repository: `curl -u owner:ownerpass123 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{'name':'draft-asset-demo','private':false,'auto_init':true}' '$BASE/api/v1/user/repos'` 3. As `owner`, create a draft release and copy the returned numeric release ID: `curl -u owner:ownerpass123 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{'tag_name':'draft-1','name':'draft-1','draft':true}' '$BASE/api/v1/repos/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases'` 4. Create a harmless asset with recognizable content: `printf 'draft-only-binary' > /tmp/draft-asset.txt` 5. Upload it to the draft release and copy the returned `uuid` or `browser_download_url`: `curl -u owner:ownerpass123 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' --data-binary @/tmp/draft-asset.txt '$BASE/api/v1/repos/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases/$RELEASE_ID/assets?name=draft-asset.txt'` 6. As an anonymous user with no cookies, verify the draft release itself is hidden: `curl -i '$BASE/api/v1/repos/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases/$RELEASE_ID'` 7. Confirm this returns `404`. 8. As the same anonymous user, request the generic attachment route: `curl -i '$BASE/attachments/$UUID'` 9. Observe `200 OK` and the file body `draft-only-binary`. 10. Optionally compare with the normal release download route `/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases/download/draft-1/draft-asset.txt`, which should remain hidden while `/attachments/$UUID` succeeds. ### Impact This leaks unpublished release assets. Anyone who learns the attachment UUID can retrieve draft binaries or other release files before the maintainer chooses to publish them.

CVE-2026-101023.title: Gitea's OAuth2 token endpoint verified the signature and grant of ...

CVE-2026-103059.title: When Gitea's built-in SSH server is enabled (`START_SSH_SERVER =  ...

CVE-2026-103504.title: Changing an organization team's permission through the API with o ...

CVE-2026-103667.title: Gitea's container registry served blob downloads with a `Content- ...

CVE-2026-103670.title: When a Gitea Actions run was inserted, older runs in the same wor ...
CVE-2026-103670.description: When a Gitea Actions run was inserted, older runs in the same workflow-level concurrency group were cancelled without checking whether the new run still needed approval. CVE-2026-59766.title: Gitea CVE-2026-20800 sibling endpoints not covered: revoked user still reads private repo objects via `/api/v1/user/starred` and private issue titles via `/api/v1/user/times`
CVE-2026-59766.description:
## Summary
CVE-2026-20800 fixed private-info leakage to revoked users only for the notification endpoint. Two
sibling endpoints that return data keyed on the caller's own relationship still do not re-check repo
access at output time:
- `GET /api/v1/user/starred` — `getStarredRepos()` computes a per-repo permission but still lists every
  starred repo (no filtering), so the full repo object (`full_name`, `private`, `clone_url`, `ssh_url`)
  of a now-inaccessible private repo is returned.
- `GET /api/v1/user/times` — `ListMyTrackedTimes()` queries by `UserID` only and `LoadAttributes` brings
  in the issue (`title`, `state`), leaking private issue titles after revocation.

## Steps to reproduce
Using the provided reproduction materials, as a revoked user:
1. Control: `GET /api/v1/repos/admin/starred-test` → **404**.
2. `GET /api/v1/user/starred` → leaks `admin/starred-test`, `private:true`, `clone_url`.
3. `GET /api/v1/user/times` → leaks `issue.title = "SECRET: …"`, `state`.

(Runtime-confirmed on `gitea/gitea:1.25.4`. Oracle = planted sentinel title; no real secret exfiltrated.)

## Impact
A former collaborator can enumerate private repos they starred and read private issue titles they logged
time on, indefinitely after access revocation. Metadata only (no repo content / comment bodies). Low.

## Suggested remediation
1. `getStarredRepos`: drop (or minimally redact) repos where `permission.HasAnyUnitAccessOrPublicAccess()`
   is false for the caller.
2. `ListMyTrackedTimes`: filter tracked-time entries by current repo access.
3. Optionally clear a user's stars / time entries for a private repo on revocation.

## Credit
Reported as part of an incomplete-patch measurement study (responsible disclosure).
